subtype: Approach: involving a trusted adult even against a request for secrecy [Action]
passage: Yamini's message came in at lunch: she didn't see the point in anything anymore, and Anirban had to swear he would tell nobody. His hands went cold. He had kept every promise he had ever made her, some of them silly. But he kept hearing how flat her words sounded. After the last bell he walked to the counsellor's room instead of the bus stop. Mrs Kulkarni put down her pen and listened without interrupting. She told him that this was not betrayal and he had done the right thing, and said she would speak with Yamini and her parents that same evening. At home Anirban told his father everything too. His father sat beside him, thanked him, and stayed while Anirban typed: "I'm not angry with you. I told people who can help. I'm still your friend."

qa.q: Who did Anirban tell at school?
qa.a: Anirban told the counsellor, Mrs Kulkarni.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling as he chose to break the promise?
qa.a: He felt frightened and torn: his hands went cold, but the flat sound of Yamini's words worried him more than the promise.

qa.q: What could Anirban do alongside telling the adults, and why?
qa.a: He could keep checking in as a friend, as his message shows, because it keeps trust alive while adults handle the proper help.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel when the counsellor and her parents get involved?
qa.a: Yamini may feel angry or exposed at first, but Anirban's message that he is not angry and is still her friend gives her a reason to believe he acted from care.

grounding: The teen tells the counsellor and his father despite the promise, believing his friend's safety matters more and adults can arrange help.

subtype: Approach: involving a trusted adult even against a request for secrecy [Action]
passage:
“Amma, can I tell you something? Urmila made me promise not to.”
“Sit, Lokesh. Tell me.”
“She's been cutting classes. Today she said she feels like she can't go on, and that I mustn't tell anyone. She begged me.”
Amma put down the vegetables. “What did you do?”
“I went to Mrs Rao, the counsellor, after lunch. I felt like a traitor walking in. But I thought, if something happens to her, the promise won't matter. Her being safe matters more than her being angry with me.”
“And Mrs Rao?”
“She called Urmila in straight away and phoned her parents. She said they'll arrange proper help. And she told me to tell you too, tonight.”
Amma took his hand. “You did the right thing. If she's angry, she can be angry and safe. I'll call Urmila's mother now as well, just to be sure she's home with her.”
“Thank you, Amma.”

qa.q: Who did Lokesh go to after lunch?
How did Lokesh feel walking into the counsellor's room?
qa.a: Lokesh felt like a traitor, torn between the promise and fear for Urmila's safety.

qa.q: What else could Lokesh do if Urmila is angry with him tomorrow?
qa.a: Tell her calmly he did it because he cares, and stay her friend, while leaving the help itself to the adults.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Amma?
qa.a: Amma is alarmed but proud, and acts straight away by calling Urmila's mother to make sure she is safe at home.

grounding: Shows a teen telling the school counsellor and his own parent despite a friend's plea for secrecy, reasoning that her safety matters more than the promise.

subtype: Approach: involving a trusted adult even against a request for secrecy [Action]
passage:
Last spring my best friend Dolma told me, on the bus home, that she'd been thinking about not being alive any more. Then she grabbed my wrist. “Promise you won't tell anyone. Promise, Sahil.”
I said I couldn't promise that. She cried and called me a traitor. I felt like one.
But I kept thinking: I'm fifteen. I can't keep her safe on my own, and adults can do things I can't. Her being safe mattered more than her being angry.
Papa was waiting at our stop. I told him right there, and he phoned Dolma's mother before we had even crossed the road. The next morning I went to Mrs Kapoor, the school counsellor, too, and she arranged for Dolma to see someone properly.
Dolma didn't speak to me for eleven days. On the twelfth she sat next to me at lunch and said, “I'm still annoyed. But thanks."

qa.q: How many days did Dolma not speak to Sahil?
How did Sahil feel when Dolma called him a traitor?
qa.a: Sahil felt like a traitor too, hurt and torn, even while sure that telling was right.

qa.q: Why did Sahil tell both Papa and the counsellor?
qa.a: Papa could act that evening by calling Dolma's mother, and the counsellor could arrange proper ongoing help.

qa.q: How might Dolma see Sahil's choice by the twelfth day?
qa.a: Dolma is still annoyed but grateful, seeing that Sahil broke the secret because he cared about her safety.

grounding: Shows a teen telling his parent and the school counsellor despite a friend begging for secrecy, reasoning that her safety outweighs a promise.
